Coventry.wildlife_intro:
Coventry's lake and its mill village give our crew its two main storylines. Around Coventry Lake, raccoons den in cottage chimneys and under decks, bats summer in cottage attics, and muskrats work the shoreline. In South Coventry and across the farm roads, squirrels and bats use the older homes and barns, woodchucks burrow at field edges and under sheds, and the Willimantic and Skungamaug Rivers move beavers, mink, and otters through town — mostly seen, occasionally a flooding complaint where a brook is dammed.

Lake cottages opened in spring deserve a chimney and attic check before the family settles in; a quiet winter is an invitation to raccoons and squirrels. Our crew inspects cottages and year-round homes alike, removes animals humanely, and seals entries so the place holds between visits. Village and farm properties often need barns and sheds included in the plan. Fall sealing across Coventry keeps the lake houses and the farmhouses equally quiet through the cold months.

Crystal Lake adds the shore version of the same work — raccoons and bats in cottages, muskrats at the shoreline — while squirrels and mice are a constant in the subdivisions growing around the center.

On farm properties our crew thinks beyond the house: feed storage, coop construction, and barn entries decide whether removing one raccoon solves anything. We remove problem animals humanely, seal the buildings that matter, and give practical advice on the rest. Lake homeowners get a spring cottage check, and everyone benefits from fall sealing before rodents claim the warm spaces. Ellington rewards the full-property approach — animals here have options, and closing only one rarely ends the story.

Stafford.wildlife_intro:
Stafford is one of Connecticut's most wooded towns, and wildlife is simply the neighborhood. In Stafford Springs, raccoons, squirrels, and bats use the older mill-era homes along the Willimantic River, while out in Staffordville and West Stafford the calls involve barns, woodpiles, and porcupines chewing outbuildings. Woodchucks work the clearings and gardens, fishers are heard and occasionally seen in the Shenipsit woods, and beavers dam brooks that flood low roads and yards a few times a year somewhere in town.

Our crew's Stafford work is about making a house a firm boundary in a wild landscape: inspect the roofline, chimney, and foundation, remove what has moved in, and seal it so the forest stays outside. Outbuildings get the same attention, because a bat barn or a raccoon shed next to a sealed house is unfinished business. Fall is the critical season — every animal in these hills is choosing winter quarters, and a Stafford home closed up in October is the goal we work toward with each customer.

Tolland.wildlife_intro:
Tolland's homes sit in the woods, and our calls here reflect a town built inside wildlife habitat. Squirrels and flying squirrels enter the attics of subdivisions that back onto forest, raccoons den in chimneys from the Green to Grant Hill, and bats summer in the historic center's older houses and in barns across town. Woodchucks clear burrows under sheds at woodland edges, porcupines occasionally chew outbuildings, and the Willimantic River headwaters and Shenipsit Lake shore bring beavers and muskrats to the wet corners of town.

The pattern we see is that woods-edge homes get tested constantly — an entry sealed is an entry kept, but new gaps from settling, storms, and chewing need watching. Our crew inspects thoroughly, removes animals humanely, and seals with materials that stand up to determined squirrels. We also advise on the tree limbs and vents that give animals their routes in. Fall sealing matters most here, because Tolland winters are cold and every attic in town is being evaluated by something with fur by October.

Vernon.wildlife_intro:
Vernon combines a mill city and a suburb in one town, and our crew works both. In Rockville, raccoons and bats use the mill-era chimneys and rooflines, rats work the older basements and commercial blocks, and squirrels are in the triple-deckers as readily as in single-family homes. In the suburban south and west, the calls are attic squirrels, woodchucks under decks, and skunks in lawns, while Shenipsit Lake and the Tankerhoosen corridor keep woods and water at the edges of the eastern neighborhoods.

Rockville's shared structures need building-wide inspections — sealing one unit in a connected mill-era row rarely holds. Our crew plans those jobs as single projects, removes the animals, and seals across the structure. Suburban homes get thorough roofline and foundation work. Spring denning fills Rockville chimneys, summer brings bats and woodchucks, and fall sends mice and squirrels looking for winter space across Vernon — the season when our sealing work does the most good for the year ahead.
